samples.text:
NOTICEDESK: BRAND MESSAGING FRAMEWORK
Internal reference for writers, sales and agencies. Not customer-facing copy. Version 1.

1. AUDIENCE AND PROBLEM

Who we serve. Chartered accountancy firms with 3 to 30 staff in tier-2 cities such as Jaipur. Two people inside each firm matter:

- The partner. Signs the replies, owns the client relationship and is the one a client calls when a notice is missed. Usually the buyer.
- The article manager or senior staff member. Keeps the tracker, chases clients for documents and drafts the reply. The daily user.

What they use today. An Excel sheet with one row per notice, WhatsApp groups where clients forward notices as photos and PDFs, and the partner's memory. That is the alternative we are positioned against.

The problem. A GST or income-tax notice is a dated obligation. When it lives in a WhatsApp photo and a spreadsheet row that nobody updated, the firm learns its status when the client phones or the due date has passed. The sheet is only as current as the last person who edited it.

Customer language: [proof needed: 10 to 15 verbatim phrases from partner and article-manager interviews, with source and date. Until these exist, do not put words in a customer's mouth in any copy.]

2. POSITIONING STATEMENT

For CA partners and article managers in tier-2 cities who track GST and income-tax notices in Excel and WhatsApp, NoticeDesk is the notice-tracking software for CA firms that gives every notice one record, one named owner and one due date. Unlike a spreadsheet that depends on whoever edited it last, NoticeDesk logs each notice once and reminds its owner before the reply is due.

3. UMBRELLA MESSAGE

Every notice has an owner and a due date, and the whole firm can see both. (15 words)

4. MESSAGE PILLARS

Pillar 1: One register for every GST and income-tax notice
Notices reach a firm as WhatsApp forwards, emails and portal downloads. NoticeDesk gives them one place to live. Each record holds the client, the type of notice, the date issued, the reply due date and the current status. Nobody has to search a chat to find out where a client stands.
Proof points:
- Product fact: every notice record carries client, notice type, issue date, reply due date and status. Source: product specification [confirm field list with product team].
- [proof needed: number of notices logged by pilot firms and over what period]
- [proof needed: time to find one client's notice status before and after, from pilot-firm interviews]

Pillar 2: One named owner and one due date on every notice
A notice with no owner is everyone's problem and therefore nobody's. NoticeDesk will not save a notice without one assigned person and one reply date. The owner is reminded before the date, and an overdue notice shows in red for the whole firm.
Proof points:
- Product fact: a record cannot be saved without an owner and a due date. Source: product specification [confirm].
- [proof needed: reminder schedule as built, for example how many days before the due date]
- [proof needed: replies filed after the due date at pilot firms, before and after NoticeDesk]

Pillar 3: The partner sees every open notice without asking anyone
A partner should not need to ask three staff members which notices are open. One screen lists every open notice by client, owner and due date, oldest due date first. Before a client meeting, the partner opens the client's page and sees the full notice history.
Proof points:
- Product fact: a partner view of all open notices, sortable by due date, owner and client. Source: product specification [confirm].
- [proof needed: partner quote on replacing the weekly "which notices are pending?" round of calls, with permission to name them]

5. SEGMENT MATRIX

| | Partner | Article manager / staff |
|---|---|---|
| Top pain | Hears about a missed notice from the client | Maintains the sheet and gets blamed when it is stale |
| Lead pillar | 3: sees every open notice without asking | 2: one owner, one due date, reminders |
| Key message | "You will know which notices are open before your client asks." | "Log it once. NoticeDesk reminds you, so you stop chasing your own sheet." |
| Typical objection | "Excel already works for us." | "Another tool means more data entry." |
| Next step to ask for | A 20-minute walkthrough with last month's notices loaded | Log 5 live notices in one sitting and see the reminders |

6. BOILERPLATES

About 10 words:
NoticeDesk helps CA firms track every GST and income-tax notice.

About 50 words:
NoticeDesk is a Jaipur software company that helps chartered accountancy firms track GST and income-tax notices. Each notice gets one record, one named owner and one due date, so partners see what is open and staff stop depending on Excel sheets and WhatsApp forwards. It is built for firms with 3 to 30 staff.

About 100 words:
NoticeDesk is a Jaipur software company that helps chartered accountancy firms track GST and income-tax notices. Most firms with 3 to 30 staff still keep notices in an Excel sheet and WhatsApp groups. NoticeDesk replaces both with one register. Each notice gets one record, one named owner and one reply due date, and the owner is reminded before the date. Partners see every open notice on one screen, sorted by due date, and can open any client's full notice history before a meeting. NoticeDesk does not file replies on the government portals; the firm still does that. [founded year and number of firms using it: proof needed]

7. OBJECTIONS AND APPROVED ANSWERS

1. "Excel already works for us."
Answer: Excel works while the person who keeps it is in the office and every notice gets typed in. It stops working when a notice stays in a WhatsApp photo or the sheet owner is on leave. NoticeDesk keeps the same shape, one row per notice, and adds an owner and a reminder.
Proof: [proof needed: a pilot firm that moved off Excel, named with consent]

2. "My staff will not use another tool."
Answer: Staff already enter the same fields in Excel today. NoticeDesk asks for the same fields, in one form, once per notice. Start by logging only new notices; old ones can follow.
Proof: [proof needed: median time for a new firm to log its first 10 notices]

3. "Is my clients' data safe?"
Answer: Give only what is confirmed: where the data is hosted, who in the firm can see which clients, and how access is removed when a staff member leaves. Do not say "secure" without those facts.
Proof: [proof needed: hosting location, access-control design, data-protection statement from the product and legal teams]

4. "Does it file the reply for us?"
Answer: No. NoticeDesk tracks notices, owners and due dates. The firm still files replies on the GST and income-tax portals, as it does today.
Proof: product scope [confirm with product team].

8. VOICE AND WORD LIST

Voice traits:
- Plain. Write as one CA would explain to another over chai. Do: "Every notice has an owner." Don't: "Streamline your compliance workflow."
- Specific. Use the field names, the notice types and the due date. Do: "Reply due 14 June, owner: Ritu." Don't: "Stay on top of deadlines."
- Calm. CAs are careful readers and distrust hype. Do: "reminds the owner before the date." Don't: "never miss a notice again."

Words to use: notice, register, owner, due date, reply, open notices, client file, partner, article, status.

Words to avoid: world-class, one-stop solution, seamless, hassle-free, "compliance made easy", "never miss", "guaranteed", "AI-powered" (until a feature is built that is), "No. 1" or "best" without a source on file. Use "notice", never "ticket" or "case"; use "reply", never "response".

9. WORKED EXAMPLE (homepage hero)

Headline: Every GST and income-tax notice, with an owner and a due date.
Subhead: NoticeDesk gives your firm one register for notices, so partners see what is open and staff stop chasing the Excel sheet.
Button: Book a 20-minute walkthrough

LASTMILE MALWA: MISSION, VISION, VALUES

MISSION
We deliver kirana-store and D2C orders the same day across Madhya Pradesh, so a small shop can keep the promise a big chain makes.

VISION
A Madhya Pradesh where no shop loses a sale because its delivery arrives tomorrow.

OUR VALUES

1. Keep the slot | वक़्त का वादा
A delivery slot is a promise to a customer, and we treat it like one.
This means we: call the customer before we miss a slot and give a new time.
We don't: mark an order delivered before it is in the customer's hand.

2. Own the parcel | पार्सल मेरा
Whoever picks up an order owns it until it is delivered or returned, whatever their job.
This means we: stay on a stuck order to the end, whether we ride a bike or write the code.
We don't: say "that is another team's problem."

3. Safety before speed | पहले सुरक्षा
No slot is worth an accident.
This means we: wear the helmet, take the break, and let a rider say "I can't make this slot" without a penalty.
We don't: plan a route so tight that skipping a signal is the only way to finish it.

4. Say it straight | सीधी बात
Shop owners and teammates get the honest answer early.
This means we: tell a kirana owner today that tomorrow's volume will not fit our routes.
We don't: accept an order we already know we cannot deliver.

HOW WE USE THESE
Every interview has one question on a value. Every missed-slot review asks which value we skipped.

प्रधानाचार्य महोदय, सभी शिक्षकगण, अभिभावकगण और मेरे प्यारे बच्चो, आप सबको नमस्कार।

खड़-खड़-खड़।

आप में से कितने लोगों ने सुबह पाँच बजे किसी दुकान का शटर उठते सुना है? मैंने सुना है। रोज़ सुना है। गया जंक्शन के पास हमारी साइकिल मरम्मत की एक छोटी-सी दुकान थी। पापा रोज़ ठीक पाँच बजे शटर उठाते थे, और उसी आवाज़ पर मेरी आँख खुलती थी। मैं आपके ही जैसे एक सरकारी स्कूल की लड़की थी। आज मैं इस ज़िले में अफ़सर हूँ। लेकिन आज मैं आपको अपनी जीत की कहानी सुनाने नहीं आई हूँ। मैं आपको अपनी दो हार की कहानी सुनाने आई हूँ।

बारहवीं के बाद मैंने तय कर लिया था कि सिविल सर्विस की परीक्षा दूँगी। हमारे घर में न कोई अफ़सर था, न किसी अफ़सर से जान-पहचान। कोचिंग की फ़ीस हमारी दुकान की पूरे साल की कमाई से ज़्यादा थी। तो मैंने गया की पुरानी लाइब्रेरी की सदस्यता ली। सुबह माँ टिफ़िन बाँध देतीं, और मैं नौ बजे से शाम तक वहीं बैठकर पढ़ती। जब बिजली जाती, तो खिड़की के पास खिसक जाती। वहाँ की कुर्सी का एक पाया छोटा था। मुझे आज भी उसकी खट-खट याद है।

पहला प्रयास। प्रीलिम्स का रिज़ल्ट आया। मैं कट-ऑफ़ से नौ नंबर पीछे रह गई। सिर्फ़ नौ नंबर। मैं तीन दिन छत से नीचे नहीं उतरी।

उन्हीं दिनों पड़ोस की एक चाची माँ से बोलीं, "बिटिया को कितना पढ़ाओगी? अब हाथ पीले कर दो।" मैंने दरवाज़े के पीछे से सुना। माँ ने कुछ नहीं कहा। बस रोटी बेलती रहीं। अगली सुबह शटर फिर उठा, और मैं फिर लाइब्रेरी गई।

दूसरा प्रयास। इस बार प्रीलिम्स निकल गया। मैंने मेन्स दिया। मैं मन ही मन अपने आप को अफ़सर मान चुकी थी। रिज़ल्ट आया, लिस्ट में मेरा नाम नहीं था। उस दिन मैं किसी से कुछ नहीं बोली। पापा ने भी नहीं पूछा कि कितने नंबर आए। उन्होंने बस इतना कहा, "चाय पी ले, बेटा।" और एक पंक्चर टायर ठीक करने बैठ गए।

बाहर गली में बच्चे क्रिकेट खेल रहे थे। उनकी आवाज़ें मुझे किसी और दुनिया की लगती थीं।

उस रात मैं छत पर बैठी थी। हाथ में दोनों साल के पेपर थे। आम तौर पर हम सिर्फ़ इतना देखते हैं कि पास हुए या फ़ेल। उस रात मैंने पहली बार हिसाब लगाया कि नंबर कहाँ-कहाँ कटे। पहले साल भी, दूसरे साल भी, सबसे ज़्यादा नंबर एक ही जगह कटे थे। इकॉनमी।

सच यह था कि मैं इकॉनमी से भागती थी। उसमें आँकड़े थे, ग्राफ़ थे, और हिंदी में अच्छी किताब भी नहीं मिलती थी। जो विषय अच्छे लगते थे, उन्हें मैं घंटों पढ़ती रही। जो विषय डराता था, उसे कल पर टालती रही। मैं मेहनत की कमी से नहीं हारी थी। मैं अपने टालने से हारी थी।

उस रात मैंने एक बहुत छोटा फ़ैसला किया। बाक़ी सब वैसा ही चलेगा। पर रोज़ सुबह, शटर की आवाज़ के बाद, सबसे पहले तीस मिनट सिर्फ़ इकॉनमी। नींद आए तो भी। मन न करे तो भी। सिर्फ़ तीस मिनट।

पहले हफ़्ते मैं एक ही ग्राफ़ पर बीस मिनट अटकी रही। नौवें दिन मैं सो गई और आधा घंटा छूट गया। मैंने खुद से कहा, कोई बात नहीं, कल फिर से। और अगली सुबह मैं फिर बैठी। एक महीने के आख़िर में मैंने एक ग्राफ़ देखा और मुझे डर नहीं लगा। मैं छत पर अकेले हँस पड़ी। अगले साल, तीसरे प्रयास में, लिस्ट में मेरा नाम था। बाक़ी विषय मैंने वैसे ही पढ़े जैसे पहले पढ़ती थी। फ़र्क़ सिर्फ़ इतना था कि अब दिन का पहला काम वह होता था जिससे डर लगता था।

हार ने मुझे एक चीज़ दी, हिसाब। पता चला कि मैं कहाँ कमज़ोर हूँ। जो अपनी कमज़ोरी का नाम जानता है, उसके पास आधा रास्ता पहले से होता है।

आज मैं आपको एक ही बात देकर जा रही हूँ। छोटा काम, रोज़। बड़ा नतीजा, एक दिन।

अब आपकी बात, बच्चो। आप में से कोई गणित से डरता है। कोई अंग्रेज़ी बोलने में अटक जाता है। किसी को केमिस्ट्री के रिएक्शन याद नहीं रहते। किसी का बोर्ड परीक्षा का नाम सुनते ही दिल बैठ जाता है। मैं जानती हूँ, क्योंकि मैंने भी यही किया था। जो मुश्किल लगता है, हम उसे कल पर छोड़ देते हैं, और कल कभी आता नहीं।

और आज तो कल को निगलने वाली चीज़ हम सबकी जेब में है। रील के दो घंटे चुटकी में निकल जाते हैं, और गणित के दस मिनट पहाड़ लगते हैं। मैं फ़ोन को बुरा नहीं कह रही। मैं बस इतना कह रही हूँ कि जो डराता है, उसे सबसे पहले पढ़िए, फ़ोन उसके बाद।

कुछ बच्चे सोच रहे होंगे कि हमारे पास न कोचिंग है, न ट्यूशन, न घर पर पढ़ने की अलग जगह। मेरे पास भी नहीं थी। मेरे पास एक टूटी कुर्सी थी और तीस मिनट थे। तीस मिनट हर किसी के पास होते हैं।

इसलिए मैं आपसे सिर्फ़ एक चीज़ माँगती हूँ। आज रात सोने से पहले एक विषय चुनिए। वही, जिससे आपको सबसे ज़्यादा डर लगता है। आज से अगले तीस दिन, रोज़ तीस मिनट, सिर्फ़ उसी विषय की सेल्फ़-स्टडी। फ़ोन दूसरे कमरे में। एक कॉपी में रोज़ एक टिक। कोई दिन छूट जाए, तो मेरी तरह कहिए, कोई बात नहीं, कल फिर से। तीस दिन बाद टिक गिनिए, और वह कॉपी अपने शिक्षक को दिखाइए। बस इतना।

कल सुबह जब आपके मोहल्ले में किसी दुकान का शटर उठे, तो वह आवाज़ याद कीजिएगा। वह शटर किसी के मूड का इंतज़ार नहीं करता। रोज़ उठता है। मेरे पापा का शटर बीस साल में एक दिन भी देर से नहीं उठा, और उसी शटर ने मुझे यहाँ तक पहुँचाया। आप सबके पास भी एक शटर है। आपके तीस मिनट।

छोटा काम, रोज़। बड़ा नतीजा, एक दिन।

धन्यवाद।

RBI cuts repo rate by 25 basis points: what it means for your home-loan EMI

Floating-rate borrowers should pay less interest, but not on the day of the cut. Here is who gains, who does not and what to check with your lender.

Updated on [date]

WHAT HAPPENED
The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee cut the repo rate by 25 basis points, or 0.25 percentage points, on [date of announcement]. The rate moved from [old repo rate]% to [new repo rate]%, according to the RBI's policy statement [verify against the statement]. The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks. When it falls, loans linked to it become cheaper. For a salaried borrower with a floating-rate home loan, that means either a smaller EMI or a shorter loan.

KEY POINTS
- The repo rate is down 25 basis points as of [date].
- Home loans linked to the repo rate get cheaper when the lender next resets the rate, not on the day of the cut.
- On an illustrative Rs 30 lakh, 20-year loan, the EMI falls by about Rs 473 a month [verify].
- Fixed-rate loans do not change. Existing fixed deposits keep their rate; new deposits may pay less.
- Banks, not the RBI, decide how quickly they pass on the cut.

BACKGROUND
Since October 2019, banks have been required to link new floating-rate home loans to an external benchmark, and most lenders use the repo rate [verify]. A borrower's rate is the benchmark plus the lender's own spread. So when the repo rate falls 25 basis points, the loan rate should fall 25 basis points once the lender resets it. Lenders must reset at least once every three months [verify against the RBI circular]. Older loans linked to a bank's own MCLR adjust more slowly and not in step with the repo rate [verify]. Before this cut the repo rate stood at [old repo rate]%, after [one line on the previous move, from the MPC statement].

HOW IT WORKS
The chain is short. The RBI cuts the repo rate. The benchmark that the loan is tied to falls. At the next reset date the loan's interest rate falls. The lender then lowers the EMI or shortens the loan. RBI rules on resets say the borrower should be told the options [verify the current circular].

Worked example. This uses an illustrative loan rate of 8.50% before the cut and 8.25% after. It is not any bank's actual rate.

Loan: Rs 30,00,000 over 20 years (240 months).
- EMI at 8.50%: about Rs 26,035.
- EMI at 8.25%: about Rs 25,562.
- Difference: about Rs 473 a month, or about Rs 5,700 a year [verify].

Over the full 20 years, if the rate stays at 8.25%, total interest falls from about Rs 32.48 lakh to about Rs 31.35 lakh. That is roughly Rs 1.13 lakh less [verify].

If the borrower keeps paying the old EMI of Rs 26,035, the loan ends about 10 to 11 months earlier [verify]. Choosing to keep the EMI is the cheaper route over the life of the loan, because every extra rupee goes to principal.

WHO IS AFFECTED
Existing borrowers on repo-linked floating loans. The rate falls at the next reset date. The date is in the sanction letter or the lender's app.

Existing borrowers on MCLR-linked loans. The change reaches them slowly. They can ask the lender to move to a repo-linked rate, which often carries a fee [verify].

Borrowers on fixed-rate loans. Nothing changes.

New borrowers. New loans will be priced off the lower repo rate, but the spread depends on the borrower's credit score and the lender. Offers from at least three lenders are worth comparing.

Fixed-deposit holders. An existing FD keeps its rate until maturity. New deposits and renewals may earn less if banks cut deposit rates [verify].

WHAT WE DON'T KNOW YET
- Whether each lender will pass on the full 25 basis points, and from which date. No lender had published revised rates at the time of writing [update when announced].
- Whether the RBI will cut again. The committee's stance is [stance, from the policy statement].
- How soon banks will lower FD rates [pending lender announcements].

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT
The next MPC meeting is scheduled for [date, from the RBI calendar]. Lenders will publish revised benchmark-linked rates over the coming weeks. The next step for a borrower is to find the loan's reset date and ask the lender in writing whether the lower rate will reduce the EMI or the tenure.

SOURCES
- RBI, Statement on Monetary Policy [link, date]
- RBI circular on external-benchmark-linked lending [link] [verify]
- Lender rate notices [links when published]

CHAPTER BRIEF (internal, not for publication)
POV: Meera Sahani, 34, boatwoman, Tulsi Ghat, Varanasi. Want: get the boat ready for the first dawn ride, the only guaranteed money of the day. Obstacle: someone used the boat in the night and left evidence that points at her family, and the local police already think of the Sahanis as trouble. Change: she keeps the passport instead of handing it in. Closing hook: she lies to a policeman for the first time in her life, with the passport against her ribs.

CHAPTER ONE

The rope was tied wrong.

Meera saw it from the top step of Tulsi Ghat, still twenty feet away, with the lamp of the tea stall behind her putting a yellow smear on the water. Her father had tied this boat off with a round turn and two half-hitches for thirty years, and she had done it the same way for two, and this was something else. A fat knot, tight as a fist. The knot of someone who had only ever tied parcels.

She went down the wet steps slowly, one hand on the stone. It was ten to five and the river was the colour of old tin. Across the water the far bank had not started yet; there was only mist and the smell of woodsmoke from the burning ghats downriver, fires that never fully went out. Somewhere up the ghat a priest was clearing his throat into a microphone.

The boat was called Annapurna. Her father had painted the name himself in red enamel, and every monsoon Meera repainted the A because the river ate it first. She put a hand on the gunwale. The planks were cold and slick, and the whole boat lifted a little, as boats do, acknowledging her.

She untied the knot with her fingernails. It took a full minute. Whoever had done it had pulled with their whole weight.

"Kaun aaya raat ko?" she said under her breath, to nobody, to the boat.

She had left at seven the night before. Last ride, a family from Pune who wanted the aarti from the water, four hundred rupees, no change given because they never had change. She had bailed, turned the oars, laid the tarpaulin over the seats. She was sure of the tarpaulin. Now it lay folded on the stern thwart, neat as a hospital sheet, and Meera had never folded it that neatly in her life.

She stepped in and took the tin can from its hook and began to bail. The bilge held more water than it should. She worked the can in short, hard scoops, the way her father had taught her, never lifting the can above the gunwale so the water fell back in. Scoop, tip, scoop. At the third scoop the can knocked against something that was not wood.

She fished for her phone, put on the torch, and put her head down under the stern seat.

A clear plastic zip bag lay wedged between two ribs of the hull, with a rubber band around it, the way you would pack a phone for a monsoon. Inside there was a passport, maroon with gold lettering, and folded around the passport a strip of paper. A railway ticket, torn across the middle. She worked the bag loose. Her hands were steady. It was her mouth that had gone dry.

She did not open the bag. She turned it over in the torchlight first. The paper strip was stiff at one edge and stained a brown that had gone almost black. It was not tea, and it was not paan. Meera had seen a great deal of blood on these steps over the years: cut feet, a boy who fell off the wall, once a goat. She knew how it dried.

She pressed the zip open and took out the passport and read the cover in the torchlight. REPUBLIQUE FRANCAISE. Inside, a photograph of a woman of about thirty with cropped dark hair, looking at the camera as if she had been told not to smile and was thinking about it. MARCHAND, Elise. Born 1991. The ticket was a sleeper from Varanasi Junction to New Delhi, seat forty-one, for the 6:10 train that morning.

Meera looked at her phone. 4:56.

"Didi!"

She almost dropped the bag. Lakhan was on the steps with two kulhads of tea held against his chest, the way he carried them every morning, not spilling a drop because he walked on the very edge of every step. He was fourteen and had been working her boat since the summer. He came down the steps in three bounces and stopped.

"Kya hua?"

"Kuch nahi." She put the passport and the ticket back into the bag and pushed it under her knee, which was a stupid thing to do, because Lakhan had eyes like a heron.

"Ye kya hai, didi?"

"Chai de."

"Wo kya hai? Pehle batao." He put the kulhads on the step. "Passport hai. Videshi ka."

Meera sat back on her heels. There was no point. She held out the ticket, edge up, so he would see the brown.

Lakhan went quiet. When he spoke, his voice was an octave down. "Khoon?"

"Pata nahi."

"Raat ko kisi ne nao khol di thi, didi. Humne to bandhi thi."

"Haan."

He picked up a kulhad and gave her one and held the other himself, as if they were at a funeral. They drank in silence. Mist moved on the water in slow rolls.

"Thana mein de dete hain," he said at last. "Inaam bhi mil sakta hai. Videshi ka passport hai."

"Tu Raju ko bhool gaya?" she said.

The boy looked at his tea.

Three years ago the Dashashwamedh police had come to the ghat in the afternoon and taken her brother out of a chai queue with two constables holding each arm. A ganja raid, they called it. Raju had held a packet for a friend, or he had not, nobody ever settled that. They kept him eleven days. There was never a charge, never a court date. Then one evening he was simply on the steps again, thinner, with a shaved head and a way of looking at uniforms that he had not had before. But his name stayed in the thana register like a stain on a sari, and every Diwali afterwards the munshi had "checked" Meera's boat licence three times. Her father said nothing for two years and then said one thing, when he was ill. He said: "Jo thana ke paas jata hai, thana use rakh leta hai."

A Sahani with a foreigner's passport and a blood-stained ticket was not a good citizen who had found something. She was a story somebody at the thana would enjoy telling.

"Phek do, didi," Lakhan said softly. He tilted his head at the river. "Ganga ji mein. Kisi ko pata nahi chalega."

"Mujhe pata chalega."

"Aur agar uss madam ko kuch ho gaya hai?"

"Isiliye to," Meera said, and heard how tired she sounded.

"Bhola chacha ko dikha lo," he said. "Wo samajhdaar hain."

Bhola Nishad's boat was tied two berths down, and he was already awake, as he had been awake before dawn every day since before Meera was born. He sat on his own stern with a bidi, wrapped in a grey shawl, his face a map of cracks. He took the bag from her without a word and read the passport name with his lips moving. Then he held the ticket stub up to the lamp for a long time.

"Kal raat ek motor-wali nao thi," he said. "Dus ke baad. Batti band."

"Kahan?"

"Assi ki taraf se aayi, idhar tak. Do log. Ek lamba tha. Hass raha tha. Angrezi mein." He drew on the bidi. "Wo nao tumhari nao ke paas rukhi nahi. Par kuch der baad wapas jaate samay uski awaaz dheeli thi. Jaise bojh kam ho gaya ho."

"Aapne kisi ko bataya?"

"Kisko?" Bhola gave her a flat look. "Thana ko?"

They both let that sit.

"Beti," he said finally, and handed the bag back. "Jo mila hai, ghar mat le jaana. Thana ya Ganga. Teesra raasta nahi hota."

"Aur agar teesra raasta ho?"

"To wo raasta tumhare liye bahut mehnga padega," he said, and turned back to his tea.

It was five-twenty. The sky behind the far bank had started to go the colour of the inside of a shell. In forty minutes the first tourists would come down the steps, in jackets, with cameras, wanting to see the sunrise from a boat, and some of them would be foreigners, and every one of them would be a possible witness. A woman in a cropped haircut was somewhere on this river's edge without her passport, and she had a train at ten past six.

She stood with the bag against her ribs and made herself think it through, since there was nobody left to do it for her. If she threw it in the river, the passport was gone, and so was whatever it might say, and a woman would stand on some platform with a train leaving and nothing in her hand. If she took it to the thana, it would be a Sahani who had found it, and a Sahani who found things was a Sahani who knew things. There was a third choice, which was the one her father would have taken: do nothing, loudly, until the matter went away. It had never once worked for him either.

Meera made up her mind in the way she had made up her mind about things since her father died: not by deciding but by finding she was already walking. She told Lakhan to hold the boat. She wrapped the bag in her father's old gamchha, still smelling of his coconut oil after two years in the locker, and put it inside her kurta against her ribs. Then she climbed the steps with her chin up, towards the chowki at the top of the ghat where a single constable sat on a plastic chair with a thermos.

She was ten steps from him when she opened the passport again to check the photograph against the face she had imagined for it, because she wanted to be sure she could describe her. A slip of paper had slid out of the back cover. It was torn from a notebook, folded in four, and the writing on it was in blue ballpoint, in English capitals pressed hard into the page.

SHIVPRASAD SAHANI. BOAT 14. TULSI GHAT. ASK FOR HIM ONLY.

Meera stopped moving.

Her father was dead. He had been dead two years in March, and his name had been scraped off the licence board in the district office eight months after that, because the form for the transfer cost four hundred rupees and she had been late. There was nobody in Kashi who would ask for him now. And there was nobody in France who should know that he had ever lived.

Under the name, smaller, in a different pen and a rougher hand, someone had added a date. It was eleven days ago, the week her father's old ledger had gone missing from the locker, the week she had blamed Raju for taking it.

She read it three times. Then she folded the paper along its old folds, put it back where it had been, and zipped the bag.

She had meant to hand it over. She could still hand it over. The constable on the plastic chair had looked up, and she saw him place her: Sahani, the boat, the brother. A small, bored interest came into his face.

But she thought: the moment I put this on his table, the name on the slip goes into a register, and the register goes to the munshi, and the munshi has had my family's name in his pocket for years.

She thought: this woman wrote my father's name, and I do not know why.

"Haan, didi?" the constable said. He had the dull, pleasant voice of a man who did not expect the day to contain anything. "Kuch kaam tha?"

Meera's hand was on the gamchha under her kurta. She felt the plastic edge of the bag against her skin, and under it her own pulse.

"Nahi," she said. "Bas dekh rahi thi. Aaj bheed kaisi rahegi."

He nodded, losing interest. He unscrewed the thermos and poured. Behind her, from the direction of Assi, she heard the sound of a motorbike on the steps, which was not allowed, and then a second engine, and then the squeal of a police jeep's tyres on wet stone. She turned. Two more constables were coming down the ghat, not hurrying, one of them thumbing at a phone.

The older one stopped in front of her and held the phone out. On the screen was a passport photograph she had looked at ten minutes ago: the cropped hair, the almost-smile.

"Isko dekha hai? Aaj subah, ya raat ko? Videshi mahila hai. Missing."

Meera looked at the screen. Then she looked up at him. She had never in her life lied to a policeman. She did it now in her father's voice, flat and kind and tired, the voice he used on tourists who asked if the river was clean.

"Nahi, sahab," she said. "Kabhi nahi dekha."

QUARTERLY STRATEGY AND OKR MEMO
Appointment-booking SaaS for clinics, Kochi (30 people) | Quarter: 1 October to 31 December 2026
Author: CEO | Audience: leadership team | Status: for decision at the leadership meeting

1. SUMMARY

Single-doctor clinics leave us at about 6% a month, and WhatsApp referrals from those same clinics bring in about 60% of our new signups. Two of our sales hires are also leaving. This quarter we stop trying to out-sell the leak. We will keep the clinics we already have, turn them into a reliable source of referrals and keep new revenue from falling while the sales team is thin. Our three results: cut single-doctor churn from about 6% to 4% a month by December. Lift referral-led signups by 20% over the September baseline. Hold new monthly recurring revenue at or above its September level in November and December.

2. DIAGNOSIS

Churn. About 6% of single-doctor clinics cancel each month. At that rate roughly half of the clinics we sign today are gone within a year (0.94 to the power of 12 is about 0.48). The clinics that leave are the ones most likely to send a colleague our way, so churn costs us the customer and the next customer.

Growth engine. About 60% of new signups arrive through WhatsApp referrals, which means growth depends on doctors recommending us to other doctors. That is cheap and it converts well, but it only works while current clinics are happy and while someone asks them to refer.

Sales capacity. Two sales hires are leaving. Because only about 40% of signups come from other channels, the exit hurts but does not stop growth. It does remove our ability to follow up leads from outside the referral network.

What we do not know. We have no clean record of why clinics cancel. Plausible causes are slow onboarding, a front desk that never adopts the tool, price, or a clinic that closes or merges. [Cause of churn: unknown until exit calls are logged.] The referral share also relies on how signups are tagged at the source [verify that every signup has a source recorded].

3. GUIDING CHOICE

We will fix retention first and let referrals carry growth, instead of rebuilding the sales team to chase multi-doctor clinics.

Alternatives considered. Option A: backfill both sales roles and push outbound to multi-doctor clinics. It treats the smaller problem and leaves a 6% monthly leak. Option B (chosen): retention, then referrals, with one sales backfill. Option C: do both fully. A 30-person team cannot staff it without dropping product quality.

We will not:
- Backfill both sales roles. We will hire one.
- Build features for multi-doctor clinic chains this quarter.
- Spend on paid ads.
- Offer discounts to stop a clinic from cancelling. We will ask why it is leaving first.
- Start work in a new city or a new clinic segment.

4. OBJECTIVES

O1. Single-doctor clinics stay with us.
O2. Happy clinics bring in other clinics, on purpose.
O3. New revenue does not fall while the sales team is thin.

5. KEY RESULTS

O1. Single-doctor clinics stay with us
- KR1.1: Monthly churn among single-doctor clinics from about 6% (September 2026) to 4% (December 2026). Owner: Head of Customer Success. Source: billing system.
- KR1.2: Share of new single-doctor clinics that reach [activation event: to be defined by 15 October] within 30 days of signup, from [baseline] to 60% for clinics signed in December. Owner: Head of Customer Success. Source: product analytics.
- KR1.3: Cancellation reason recorded for at least 90% of clinics that leave, from none today, by 15 November. Owner: Head of Customer Success. Source: exit-call log.

O2. Happy clinics bring in other clinics
- KR2.1: Referral-led new paid clinics per month from [September baseline] to [baseline plus 20%] in December. Owner: Head of Growth. Source: signup source field.
- KR2.2: Share of active clinics that sent at least one referral in the quarter, from [baseline] to [target, set after baseline is measured] by 31 December. Owner: Head of Growth. Source: referral link and WhatsApp share logs.
- KR2.3: Referral-to-paid conversion from [baseline] to [target] by 31 December. Owner: Head of Growth. Source: CRM.

O3. New revenue does not fall
- KR3.1: New monthly recurring revenue from new clinics at or above [September level] in both November and December. Owner: CEO. Source: billing system.
- KR3.2: Every open deal from the two departing reps has a named new owner within 7 days of the rep's last day. Baseline: not applicable. Owner: CEO. Source: CRM.
- KR3.3: Demo-to-paid conversion for non-referral leads from [baseline] to [target] by 31 December. Owner: CEO. Source: CRM.

6. INITIATIVES (tasks, not results)

For O1: start exit calls within 7 days of every cancellation. Define the activation event. Send a day-3 and day-10 WhatsApp check-in to each new clinic's front desk. Call any clinic with no bookings for 10 days.
For O2: ask for a referral after a clinic's first [number] bookings; write a one-line WhatsApp message a doctor can forward; decide by 15 October whether to offer a referral thank-you and what it costs.
For O3: write a handover note for every open deal; hire one sales backfill; route unowned leads to the CEO until the hire starts.

7. RISKS AND DEPENDENCIES

Churn may come from price or product fit, not onboarding. Early warning: exit calls point to price in more than a third of cases [threshold to confirm]. Response: re-diagnose before spending more on onboarding. A referral push on an unhappy base could backfire, so O2 starts after the first two weeks of exit-call data. The sales exits may take contacts and context with them; the handover notes must be done before each last day. We also depend on product analytics and the source field being accurate.

8. REVIEW CADENCE

Owners update every KR each Monday in a 30-minute leadership check-in. The CEO scores the KRs on 1 November, 1 December and 5 January, from 0.0 to 1.0. The team treats 0.7 as a good result for stretch targets and 1.0 as the standard for committed ones; KR1.3 and KR3.2 are committed, the rest are stretch. If churn is still above 5.5% on 15 November, we stop the referral push and re-run the diagnosis with the exit-call data.

Publish real-time bus data as open data, not as one more app

On [date], [announcing body] announced [app name], a new city transit app that will show [features, for example live bus locations and arrival times] for [fleet or city] [verify against the announcement]. It is a welcome step. It is also the wrong place to stop.

Stand at any Indian bus stop at eight in the morning and watch the phones come out. Riders want one answer: when does my bus arrive? Today that answer lives inside whichever app the agency chose to build or buy, and everyone else is guessing.

My position is simple. State transport corporations should publish real-time bus location and arrival data as free, open data, in a standard format, for anyone to use. The new app should be one way of reading that data, not the only way.

I have studied urban mobility in Bengaluru for [number] years at [institution], and one pattern keeps returning: [one line from the author's own work or experience, from the author's interview].

Open data reaches riders that one app cannot.
No single app serves everyone. Riders differ in language, phone, data plan and ability. A visually impaired rider needs spoken arrival alerts. A rider on a basic handset needs an SMS reply. A migrant worker may live on WhatsApp. Agencies rarely build all of these, and they should not have to. When the feed is open, developers, NGOs and the riders' own communities build them.

The precedent exists. Transport for London publishes its live feeds openly, and [number] third-party apps use them [verify with TfL]. A study commissioned by TfL put the economic value of its open data at about [amount] a year [verify: study, year, figure]. In India, Delhi's open transit data platform lets outside apps show live buses [verify current status and feed].

An open feed is also insurance. When an agency's own app crashes or its vendor contract lapses, other apps keep running because they read the same feed.

Open data lets the public check whether buses actually run.
Agencies often describe service in terms of schedules: a bus every [x] minutes on [route] [verify]. Without live data nobody outside the agency can test that. With it, a researcher, a journalist or a resident can compute how long riders actually wait, where buses bunch and which routes go empty for an hour. That is the evidence a city council needs to decide where to add buses, and the evidence the agency itself needs when it asks the state for them. [Figure from the author's own analysis or a published study on wait times or bunching, if one exists: verify.]

The strongest objection is cost and privacy.
Agencies argue that publishing costs money and creates a maintenance burden. But the expensive part, the GPS devices on the buses and the control-room server, is already paid for [verify the agency's AVL system]. Publishing a feed from it is mostly configuration, not a new system [verify with the agency's vendor]. Set that against what every private app must do today: buy or scrape the same locations on its own.

On privacy, a bus's location is not a rider's location. A well-designed feed carries the vehicle, route, trip and time. It must not carry driver or conductor IDs, and it must hold no ticketing or per-passenger data. Personal data is what the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 protects [verify the relevant provisions]; a bus's position is not that.

The objection does contain one fair point. A feed should be designed with staff identities removed and, if a safety review finds a risk on night services, delayed by a few minutes on those routes. That is a design choice. It is not a reason to keep the data closed.

What I am asking for, specifically, is this. The transport secretary of each state and the head of each city bus agency should do four things within six months [verify feasibility]. First, publish a static timetable feed and a live feed in GTFS and GTFS-Realtime, the formats most journey planners already read. Second, release both under an open licence, such as the Government Open Data Licence - India [verify], at a stable web address with no registration. Third, strip driver and conductor IDs and name one officer who is responsible for fixing broken feeds. Fourth, treat the announced app as one client of the feed. If it is good, it will win riders on its merits.

The next time a rider stands at that stop at eight in the morning, she should be able to open any app she likes and see the same fact: the bus is four minutes away.

[Author name] is an urban-mobility researcher at [institution], Bengaluru. [Disclosure: state whether the author has worked for, or received funding from, a transit-app company or the agency named above.]
